summary: Explains why some operators see odd reverse-lookup traffic from PRISONER.IANA.ORG, one of the servers in the loosely coordinated AS112 system that answers queries for private IPv4 addresses. It is meant to tell administrators who contact IANA about this that such queries are normal and expected.

eli5.summary: Some network owners see a strange name show up in their logs and worry it is an attacker. This note explains it is actually a friendly helper answering questions that should never have left the building.

questions: why am i seeing queries from prisoner.iana.org
why am i seeing replies from prisoner.iana.org
how do i stop as112 traffic
subtitle: Why a firewall may log traffic from PRISONER.IANA.ORG, and why it is usually not an attack.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and intrusion detection systems sometimes flag unexpected replies from hosts such as PRISONER.IANA.ORG, and operators often believe they are being attacked.
tldr.mechanism: The replies come from AS112 servers answering reverse-mapping DNS queries for private-use IPv4 addresses that the site itself leaked onto the public Internet. The RFC explains this and lists ways to stop the queries.
tldr.outcome: The traffic is probably no immediate danger. The only effective fix is to stop the original queries, for example by answering them locally or by running a private AS112 node.

today: RFC 6305 is an Informational document with no listed obsoleting or updating RFCs. Guidance for running an AS112 node is in RFC 6304.

sections.title: Who This Note Is For
sections.content:
RFC 6305 is written for people who saw an alarm from a firewall or an intrusion-detection system, triggered by unexpected inbound traffic. The traffic probably appeared to come from one of a few hosts named in the RFC. The published contacts for those hosts may have suggested reading this document.

The RFC does not tell readers what to do. It encourages them to follow their normal security procedures and take whatever action they consider appropriate, and it supplies information that may help.

The background is private-use addresses, the blocks that RFC 1918 sets aside for use inside individual sites. One example is 10.1.30.20. Many sites all over the world use the same ranges, so each such address only has local meaning. The host numbered 192.168.18.234 in one site almost certainly has nothing to do with a host with the same address in another site.
sections.eli5: Lots of houses on different streets are all numbered 10. The number only makes sense on your own street. This note is for people who got a surprise message and want to know who sent it.

sections.title: Reverse Mapping and the Leaked Queries
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (RFC 1034) can turn a network address into a name. The address is rearranged into a name that can be looked up, so 10.1.30.20 becomes 20.30.1.10.IN-ADDR.ARPA. A query of type PTR is built for that name and sent to a resolver. The answer usually gives a hostname, or says that none can be found. Software does this automatically, for example to add extra information to a log file, so it is largely hidden from users and administrators.

For private-use addresses the public DNS cannot give a useful answer, because the question has no global meaning. Even so, many sites are misconfigured so that these queries about their internal infrastructure are sent outside the site. From the point of view of the public DNS these queries are junk. They add unnecessary traffic to the servers that run the reverse DNS.

To isolate that traffic, dedicated servers have been deployed in many places in a loosely coordinated effort called the AS112 project. They receive and reply to these junk queries.
sections.eli5: A computer sometimes asks the phone book who lives at a number that only exists inside one house. The big phone book cannot know, so special helper desks were set up to answer these odd questions instead of bothering everyone else.

sections.title: The AS112 Servers and Why Their Replies Look Alarming
sections.content:
The RFC lists three nameservers responsible for answering queries about private-use addresses: PRISONER.IANA.ORG (192.175.48.1), BLACKHOLE-1.IANA.ORG (192.175.48.6) and BLACKHOLE-2.IANA.ORG (192.175.48.42). A request to one of them gets a response, typically a UDP datagram, although requests over TCP are perfectly valid. In both cases the packets returning to the asking site have source port 53.

If a firewall or IDS blocks these replies, a superficial review can look alarming:

  • Applications trigger the queries automatically, so firewall logs may show many policy violations over a long time.
  • Hosts whose replies are blocked often retry quickly. That can be misclassified as a denial-of-service attack. If the source ports of successive retries rise predictably, the replies can resemble a port scan.
  • An administrator who actively probes the apparent attacker, for example with a port scan, will usually cause extra inbound traffic such as a flood of ICMP messages. That can set off more alarms and hide the original problem.
sections.eli5: If you put a gate in front of the helper's reply, you keep asking again and again, and the pile of replies makes the helper look like a pest. Poking the helper back only makes more noise.

sections.title: Corrective Measures
sections.content:
A site receiving responses from these nameservers is probably under no immediate danger, and the traffic probably needs no emergency action. The RFC cannot dictate any site's security policy and accepts that many sites will have valid policies that call for stopping the responses.

The operators of the AS112 servers are not responsible for the inbound traffic. It is a response to queries sent out from the site, so the only effective way to stop it is to prevent the original queries. The RFC lists four possible measures:

  1. Stop hosts making reverse-mapping queries. Some servers can be configured not to do lookups, but across a whole site this is often hard because of the number of hosts and applications.
  2. Block the queries to AS112 servers at the site firewall. This may have unintended effects, such as long DNS lookup timeouts that make applications malfunction or make people think the network is down.
  3. Configure every DNS resolver in the site to answer authoritatively for the zones of the private-use blocks in use, so queries never go to the public DNS. Guidance is in RFC 6303.
  4. Run a private AS112 node inside the site. Guidance is in RFC 6304.
sections.eli5: You cannot stop the helper from answering. You can stop asking, answer the question yourself at home, or set up your own helper desk inside the house.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The stated purpose of the document is to help administrators correctly identify traffic from AS112 nodes and to give background so they can respond appropriately.

Hosts should never normally send queries to AS112 servers, because queries about private-use addresses should be answered locally within a site. A host that does send them may leak information about private infrastructure to the public network, which could be a security risk. The RFC also notes that the AS112 servers are a public service sanctioned by, and run in loose coordination with, the IANA, and that they are all named under IANA.ORG.
sections.eli5: The real worry is not the helper replying. It is that your questions about your own house are being shouted outside where strangers can hear them.
